My recommendation (confirmed by you): primary sample = strict AT1 + AV1 (272 people), because these two checks were built into the questionnaire at design time; “all 300” and “additionally dropping the three-page straightliners” as sensitivity analyses. Do not exclude on BEL1 (belief): it is measured after the clips and after every outcome, and “not believing” may be exactly the reaction of someone whose condition description clashed with what the clips made them feel — excluding on it would remove part of the condition effect and create selection bias. BEL1 is better used as a moderator or in a believers-only sensitivity analysis.

Covariate balance

Participants were randomised, so background variables should be similar in expectation. With finite samples, chance imbalance always occurs. The two clearest cases here: age — HA1 averages 49.7 years, H2 only 35.4; positive attitude to AI — 4.48 in A, 4.8–5.2 in every other condition. The second matters most: GAAIS positive attitude correlates r = .46 with the OH composite, so if A participants disliked AI to begin with, part of A's low scores could be “different people” rather than “different condition”. The remedy is not to drop people but to add these pre-measure variables as covariates in a secondary model and compare conclusions before and after adjustment.

Descriptive patterns (untested)

  1. Control source: A is consistently lower on the items about OriHime and the interaction. OH composite 5.34 vs H 5.61 / HA 5.71; AU1 genuineness 4.83 vs 5.52 / 5.39; CR1 warmth 5.31 vs 5.71 / 5.70. CR2 competence barely differs (5.72 vs 5.81 / 5.94). In other words the “controlled entirely by AI” description lowers trust, genuineness and warmth, not competence. A's confidence intervals are wide because it is small; whether these differences hold is for the tests to say.
  2. H and HA are almost indistinguishable — except on CR3: H 6.15 vs HA 5.74, in exactly the direction the manipulation should produce (people told “AI suggests” think the operator is in control somewhat less). This is the closest thing we have to a passed manipulation check.
  3. Operator profile: differences are small. Within H + HA, “no mention” is slightly higher on AU1 (5.63 vs 5.28 / 5.46) and CR1 (5.84 vs 5.62 / 5.66); everything else nearly coincides, with heavily overlapping intervals. In Figure 1 the real differences among H1/H2/H3 and HA1/HA2/HA3 are all inside the point clouds.
  4. Clips differ more than conditions. ADV (advice) is highest on OH (5.80), REL (chat) lowest (5.44); COL (collaboration) is lowest on AU1. A's “penalty” is largest in REL (OH 4.96 vs 5.47 / 5.57) and smallest in COL — a candidate clip × ctrl interaction. Note that the clips differ in length (70 / 105 / 115 s), so task type and duration are confounded, a design limitation.
  5. Position effects: AU1 rises from clip 1 to clip 3 (5.15 → 5.38 → 5.57), as does CR1 (5.52 → 5.59 → 5.83). Because order is balanced this does not bias condition comparisons, but it adds noise, so position belongs in the model.
  6. Attribution: in H, 73% of rows rank the human operator first for responsibility; in HA this drops to 55% while the AI gets only 16% — even with AI involved, the person is still seen as mainly responsible. In A the AI is ranked first in 58% (responsibility) and 63% (credit) of rows, the rest going to OriHime's provider and the person in the video. In HA the operator is ranked first for responsibility (55%) slightly more often than for credit (50%), a possible responsibility > credit asymmetry.
  7. Pre-measures: attitude to AI, negative attitude to robots and warmth stereotypes about people with disabilities all correlate moderately with the outcomes (|r| .3–.5). This is both a reason to expect covariates to improve precision and a reason to run attitude × condition moderation analyses.

All of the above are eyeball comparisons of means and proportions; nothing has been tested. Apparent differences (e.g. A lower) may not survive testing, and apparent non-differences (e.g. profile) may hide effects within one clip or one subgroup. The next phase turns these impressions into testable statistical questions one by one.

You confirmed that these four RQs match the design, that both factors matter, that there are no directional hypotheses and no preregistration. The table stays as the analysis matrix; the contrasts, sample and model actually used are in section 6.

Why this step matters

“Does condition A lower trust” is not directly testable; “is the expected OH composite under A lower than under H and HA, controlling for clip and position” is. Translating an RQ into a statistical question forces us to say what is compared, at which level, and controlling for what.

Phase 6 · Primary framework

Primary framework: the linear mixed model

The model

DV ~ condition + clip + position + (1 | participant)

In plain words: each person gives one score per clip. Score = the condition's average level + how easy or hard this clip is + which position it was shown in + this person's own baseline + leftover random error. (1 | participant) is “each person's own baseline”; it acknowledges that a person's three scores are correlated. What it estimates: each condition's expected score “for the same clip in the same position”; the differences between conditions are the effects we want.

Candidate methods compared

CandidateHow it treats the three clipsProblemUse in this round
Independent t-test / one-way ANOVA on the 900 rowsas 900 independent peopletriples the sample size, p-values too smallnot used
Average each person's three clips, then t-test / ANOVAone number per personlegitimate but discards clip information and cannot test clip × condition; the Welch version, which does not assume equal variances, is actually more robustrobustness check (Welch t, Mann–Whitney)
Repeated-measures ANOVAwithin-subject factorrequires sphericity; awkward with missingness (A has no CR3) and unbalanced cells; a special case of the mixed modelnot used
Linear mixed model LMMrandom intercept absorbs between-person differencesassumes equal residual variance and roughly normal residuals; treats 1–7 as equally spacedprimary model
Ordinal (proportional-odds) modeltreats 1–7 as ordered categoriesmore honest about ceiling effects; the random-effects version is immature in Python, so the GEE version is usedrobustness check (single items)

  • ICC (intraclass correlation) is .40–.78: more than half of the variation in scores comes from “different people”, not “different clips”. This is the evidence that a mixed model is required, and it explains why condition effects that look obvious in the 900-row plots are not easy to detect.
  • Residual skew −0.35 to −1.06: left-skewed (high scores piled at the top), moderate. The mixed model is not very sensitive to this, but ordinal models and the bootstrap are used to double-check.
  • Unequal variances: the most important assumption problem found in this round. Between-person spread in A is 1.3–1.5 times that in H/HA (table below, Levene p ≤ .014). The primary model assumes one variance for everyone, so for any contrast involving A the model's standard error may be too small and its p-value optimistic. Remedy: re-check with methods that do not assume equal variances (Welch t, Mann–Whitney, participant bootstrap), see section 13.

How to read the mixed-model output (OH composite as the example)

Intercept 5.47: the expected score of the reference cell (H1, clip REL, position 1). condition[A] −0.40, SE 0.22, z −1.81, p = .071: A is 0.40 points below H1; SE is the uncertainty of that estimate; z = estimate ÷ SE; p is “the probability of a z this large if the true difference were zero”. clip[ADV] +0.36, p < .001: the advice clip scores 0.36 above the chat clip, for everyone. Group Var: the variance of the between-person baselines. The paper should report: estimate, SE or CI, test statistic, p, and the variance components or ICC.

Phase 7–8 · Pairwise comparisons

All pairwise comparisons between conditions

Scope: 11 outcomes × all 21 pairs of the 7 conditions (CR3 has only 6 conditions, 15 pairs). Differences come from the primary model (clip level) or an ordinary linear model (participant level); d is standardised on the pooled SD of participant-level means. Each outcome's 21 pairs form one “statistical family”; Holm and BH corrections are applied within the family. Unadjusted raw p first, to see the complete map; but remember: with 225 comparisons and no effects at all, about 11 would still show raw p < .05.

The three control-source levels

The same model, with the cells pooled: H (3 cells, 118 people), HA (118), A (36). Pooling makes each pair more precise at the cost of hiding the profile.

Raw p, Holm p and BH p

Raw p: the p of this one comparison on its own. Holm: controls the probability of at least one false positive in the family, the strictest; three of AU1's comparisons with A survive Holm, so they stand even under the most conservative standard. BH-FDR: controls the share of false positives among the results called significant; looser than Holm, suited to an exploratory map. All three are kept; the paper states which one the main conclusions rest on.

Phase 9 · Pattern mapping

Pattern mapping

  • Unique condition: of the 84 pairwise comparisons on the four primary outcomes, 10 have raw p < .05, and every one is “some human cell > A”, in the same direction. Of the 60 comparisons among the six human cells, zero are significant. This is neither a gradient nor a cluster structure: A stands alone.
  • No profile structure: no pair within H1/H2/H3 or within HA1/HA2/HA3 is significant, and no 1 > 2 > 3 ordering is visible.
  • CR3 is a second pattern: H cells above HA cells (4 of the 9 H–HA pairs significant, no differences within H or within HA), evidence that the “AI assistance” sentence was taken in.
  • Reading the factor structure: “human vs no human” has a main effect (AU1, CR1, weaker on OH); “H vs HA” has none; “profile” has none, and there are no interactions.
  • One cell to watch: HA1 is the highest on many items (HA1 > HA3 on HM is significant). HA1 is also the oldest and most AI-positive group. One or two significant pairs among 21 cells are expected by chance; before treating it as a finding, check whether it survives covariate adjustment (section 13: the C3 difference shrinks after adjustment, consistent with this).

Do not chain p-values: “H3 > A is significant (p < .001) and HA3 > A is not (p = .06)” does not imply “H3 differs from HA3”. The direct comparison of H3 and HA3 gives p = .80, a difference of 0.02 points. One comparison crossing the line and another not is usually a matter of precision (here HA3 − A is 0.55, H3 − A is 1.09, with largely overlapping intervals). To say two effects differ, test the interaction or the “contrast of contrasts”.

Phase 11 · Contrasts

Theory-driven contrasts

Research rationale and statistical definition of each contrast: C1 the mean of the six human-involved cells vs A, answering “does telling people a human is involved change perception”; C2 the mean of the three H cells vs the three HA cells, answering “does the AI-assistance sentence itself do anything”; C3 the mean of H2, H3, HA2, HA3 vs the mean of H1, HA1, answering “does disclosing any disability change perception” — pooling presumes the two disabilities act alike, so C4 intellectual vs mobility is tested alongside; C5a/C5b split C3. All contrasts are equal-weight means of cells, so slightly unequal cell sizes do not affect them.

RQ4 · Attribution of responsibility and credit

Attribution of responsibility and credit

Method: whether an actor was ranked first is treated as a binary outcome and modelled by GEE logistic regression (participant clusters, clip as covariate), giving the odds ratio (OR) between conditions. OR = 1 means no difference; 0.5 means “the odds of being ranked first are halved”. The responsibility-vs-credit asymmetry is compared at the participant level (share of a person's three clips in which the actor was ranked first, responsibility minus credit) with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

  • HA vs H: adding “AI assistance” lowers the share ranking the human operator as most responsible from 72% to 55% (OR .47, p = .001) and as most creditable from 71% to 51% (OR .42, p < .001). The share moved away goes mainly to the AI (ranked first in about 15% of HA rows) and to the person in the video.
  • Correction for the different option sets (added after the cross-review): H offers 3 rows and HA 4, so the odds of being ranked first fall mechanically when an option is added. On a common anchor — whether the operator is ranked ahead of both “OriHime's provider” and “the person in the video” — responsibility is H 72.3% vs HA 60.7% (OR .59, p = .022) and credit 71.2% vs 60.2% (OR .61, p = .032). The shift is not purely mechanical, but “odds halved” mixes real reallocation with the added option; the paper uses the common-anchor numbers.
  • A vs HA: with no human, the share ranking the AI first jumps from 15% to 57% (responsibility) and 60% (credit), OR ≈ 7.8. On the common anchor the jump largely disappears: the AI is ranked ahead of the provider and the interlocutor in HA 52% vs A 57% (responsibility, OR 1.24, p = .47) and 49% vs 60% (credit, OR 1.60, p = .14). The AI's standing relative to the provider and the interlocutor is similar in both groups; the 7.8 mainly reflects that the person is no longer on the list.
  • Disability disclosure: OR .89 (responsibility) and .80 (credit), both non-significant: disclosing the operator's disability did not make participants assign the operator more or less responsibility.
  • Responsibility > credit asymmetry: only in HA (the operator is ranked first 4.8 points more often for responsibility than for credit, p = .024); not in H, and not for the AI in A. A very small effect, “suggestive”.

BEL1 does not differ across the 7 conditions (omnibus p = .45; C1 p = .30), so the three descriptions were believed to the same degree — the credibility check passes (it asks about the whole description, not the disability sentence, so it cannot show that the disability label was believed). It does not show that the manipulation worked; the evidence for that is CR3: people told that AI assisted rated the operator as less in control (H 6.14 vs HA 5.73, d = .40, p = .002). The AI-only condition has no direct check; the only indirect evidence is that A participants assign responsibility and credit to the AI.

Phase 13 · Robustness and sensitivity

Robustness and sensitivity analyses

Each method listed has its own rationale: alternative sample definitions (does the exclusion rule drive the conclusion); pre-measure covariates (GAAIS, NARS, SCM warmth, age — because these are imbalanced by chance after randomisation and correlate .3–.5 with the outcomes); Welch t and Mann–Whitney on participant means (no equal-variance or normality assumption); participant bootstrap (added after Levene's test found larger variance in A, a data-informed robustness check); ordinal GEE (1–7 as ordered categories, answering the ceiling effect; single items only). Cells show the difference (or odds ratio) and p.

  • The C1 effect on AU1 holds under every method (largest p .023): the only perception effect in this round that is significant under every specification.
  • The C1 effect on CR1 is significant under the model, covariate adjustment, bootstrap and ordinal GEE, and just over the line under Welch t (.052) and Mann–Whitney (.092): the difference is real but the precision limited.
  • The C1 effect on the OH composite is significant only under the equal-variance model methods (.019–.039); the variance-robust methods give p = .055–.069. It is driven by OH2 usefulness (ordinal GEE p = .031) and OH3 willingness; OH1 trustworthiness itself is not significant (p = .10–.17). So “AI control lowers trust” is not supported; “lowers usefulness and willingness” is.
  • C3 disclosure: negative under every method, p ≈ .06–.07 under the bootstrap and Welch, but after adding covariates the AU1 difference shrinks from −0.29 to −0.10 (p = .57). Part of this hint is the no-mention group happening to be older and more AI-positive; it cannot be reported as a finding, only as a direction worth replicating.
  • The exclusion rule (272 vs 300 vs 257) changes no conclusion.

E1 · Attitude × control source moderation (post hoc)

Why it is legitimate: attitudes were measured before the manipulation, so they are valid moderators; theoretically “controlled entirely by AI” is bad news for AI sceptics and not for AI enthusiasts. Statistics: an LMM with a human × attitude interaction tested by LRT; then the human − AI-only difference at 1 SD below the mean attitude, at the mean, and 1 SD above.

In the three-level test HA's slope (.30) is almost identical to H's (.26), while A's is .50: AI assistance does not trigger attitude-dependence, only “entirely AI” does.
  • For participants 1 SD below the mean attitude, the AI-only penalty is OH 0.44, AU1 0.91, CR1 0.62, CR2 0.42 points, all p ≤ .015; for participants 1 SD above, the differences lie between −0.36 and +0.20, none significant. Note: the reversed difference “AI-positive people rate the AI-controlled OriHime higher” is not itself significant and must not be written that way.
  • This also explains the unequal variances found in section 6: A's larger spread arises because attitude matters more in A.
  • Status: post hoc (it was seen once in the 09-02 report); 3 of 14 tests significant; reportable only as an exploratory finding in need of replication.

E5 · Equivalence tests (TOST)

Why it is legitimate: “p > .05” is not “the same”. TOST (two one-sided tests) asks the reverse question: is the difference small enough to fall inside a pre-specified “negligible” interval? Bounds are ±0.35 SD (the smallest effect this sample detects reliably) and ±0.50 SD (a medium effect). TOST p < .05 means “equivalence can be claimed”.

The REL-specific competence penalty: tested with the one-degree-of-freedom contrast “human × is this the chat clip”, interaction = 0.33, p = .037; but within the chat clip the ordinal model's human vs AI-only odds ratio is 1.78, p = .108. That is, the difference “AI looks less competent in the chat and not in the task clips” is barely significant, while the penalty within the chat clip is not. Status: post hoc lead.

Phases 15–21 · Paper outputs

Trial storyline and paper drafts

TRIAL. This storyline was chosen on 2026-09-04 as a working frame, not a decision. Every draft opens with a TRIAL marker and every conclusion carries an evidence-level tag (pre-specified / bounded / secondary / exploratory); keep the tags when editing.

Storyline summary

  1. Setup. The clips are identical for everyone; the only variable is one page of text: who controls, and who the operator is. Condition differences can only come from prior attribution.
  2. What human presence changes. People told “controlled entirely by AI” found the interaction less genuine (d .62, holds under every method), the controller less warm (d .52, suggestive), and OriHime less useful and less worth taking part in (suggestive); competence and trustworthiness unchanged.
  3. What does not change. The difference between human and human-with-AI operation is bounded within ±0.35 SD (OH, genuineness, warmth, hedonic motivation) or ±0.50 SD (all); explicit disability disclosure has no detectable average effect, point estimates small and negative, effects beyond half an SD excluded, no moderator found; but “AI assistance” did reduce perceived operator control (d .40), so the text was taken in.
  4. The cost lands on attribution. AI assistance lowers the odds that the operator is ranked first (raw OR .47 / .42, common-anchor OR .59 / .61); the lost share goes almost entirely to the AI (Plackett–Luce .68 → .45, AI .28); with no human the AI takes .55; in HA the operator is blamed slightly more than credited.
  5. Coda (exploratory). The AI-only penalty is concentrated among participants less positive about AI; HA's slope equals H's, so only the absence of a human triggers attitude-dependence.

Conclusions the data do not support

  • “AI-controlled robots are trusted less” — the trustworthiness item shows no difference.
  • “Disclosing a disability changes how the operator is judged” — not detected in this material; effects beyond half an SD are excluded but small-to-moderate negative effects are not; the two disabilities do not differ.
  • “AI assistance undermines the operator's standing” — perception is equivalent; only attribution shifts.
  • “The disability effect appears in particular tasks or people” — all 20 moderator tests non-significant.
  • “People who like AI prefer AI control” — the reversed difference at +1 SD is not significant.

story.md · Trial storyline

Trial storyline — "Bringing the Human Back?"

STATUS: TRIAL. Revised 2026-09-04 after an independent cross-review (analysis/study1-20260902-cross-review/): "confirmatory" is now "pre-specified (not preregistered)", equivalence claims are stated as bounds, and the disability result is a bounded null rather than evidence of no effect. This storyline was chosen on 2026-09-04 as a working frame for the Methods/Results drafts. It is not a decision. Every claim below is tagged with its evidence level; the tags must survive into the manuscript.

One-sentence thesis

Telling people that a human is behind the robot changes how genuine, warm and useful the interaction feels — but only the presence of a human matters, not whether AI assists them and not who the human is; what AI involvement does change is who gets the blame and the credit.

The arc

Act 1 — the setup (Methods). All participants watched the same three clips. The only thing that varied was one page of text: who controls OriHime (human / human with AI assistance / AI only) and, when a human was present, whether the operator was described as having an intellectual disability, a mobility disability, or not described at all. Any difference between conditions is therefore a difference in prior attribution, not in observed behaviour.

Act 2 — what human presence changes (pre-specified contrast C1). Compared with the six human-involved cells, the AI-only description made the interaction feel less genuine (d = .62, robust to every specification), the controller less warm (d = .52, suggestive: depends on the equal-variance assumption) and OriHime less useful and less worth taking part in (suggestive), while judgements of competence were unchanged. Trustworthiness itself did not differ. Allowed: "reduced perceived genuineness, warmth and usefulness." Not allowed: "reduced trust."

Act 3 — what does not change (pre-specified contrasts C2 and C3, reported as bounds). Differences between human and human-with-AI operation were bounded within ±0.35 SD for OriHime evaluation, genuineness, warmth and hedonic motivation, and within ±0.50 SD for every measure (TOST; the bounds are this design's smallest detectable effect, not a domain-derived smallest effect of interest). Explicitly disclosing that the operator has an intellectual or mobility disability, compared with not mentioning disability, produced no detectable average difference in evaluations or attributions; all point estimates were small and negative (genuineness and warmth d ≈ −.24 with intervals reaching −.5), effects larger than about half an SD are excluded, and no moderator was found among clip, contact frequency, or stereotype content. This is a bounded null for one-sentence explicit disclosure in this material, not evidence that disability status has no effect. The one measure that did respond to the AI-assistance text — perceived operator control — shows the text was read (d = .40). Allowed: "differences bounded within ±0.35/±0.50 SD"; "no detectable average effect of explicit disclosure; effects larger than about half an SD excluded." Not allowed: "identical"; "equivalent" without stating the bound and its origin; "disability has no effect"; "proves absence of bias."

Act 4 — the cost lands on attribution (pre-specified, RQ4). Adding AI assistance lowered the odds that the human operator was held most responsible (72% → 55%, OR .47) or given most credit (71% → 51%, OR .42). Because the human+AI condition offered one more actor to rank, part of that drop is mechanical; anchored on the two actors offered in every condition, the operator was ranked ahead of both the provider and the interlocutor in 72% vs 61% of rankings (OR .59 and .61), so the reallocation is real but smaller than the raw odds ratios suggest. The lost share went almost entirely to the AI (Plackett–Luce worth .28), not to the provider or the interlocutor. With no human present, the AI was ranked first in 57–60% of rankings; on the common anchor its standing relative to the provider and the interlocutor was similar with and without a human (52% vs 57%, 49% vs 60%, n.s.), so this mostly reflects the operator's absence from the list. In the human-with-AI condition the operator was slightly more likely to be blamed than credited (OR 1.21, small).

Coda — who pays the AI-only penalty (exploratory, E1). The penalty for "AI only" was concentrated among participants with less positive prior attitudes to AI (interaction with GAAIS: p = .019 for OriHime evaluation, .003 for competence; same direction on genuineness and warmth). Among AI-positive participants the two groups did not differ. The human-with-AI slope equalled the human slope: only the absence of a human triggers attitude-dependence. Allowed: "concentrated among AI-sceptical participants (exploratory)." Not allowed: "AI-positive participants preferred the AI-controlled robot."

Where each finding goes

FindingSectionLevel
AI-only lowers genuinenessResults 4.2 (primary)strong (note the item's wording is close to the manipulation; see Limitations)
AI-only lowers warmth, usefulness, willingnessResults 4.2 (primary)suggestive
Competence and trustworthiness unchangedResults 4.2null
Human vs human+AI difference boundedResults 4.3 (bounds)strong (bounded)
Explicit disability disclosure: no detectable effect, bounded within ±0.5 SDResults 4.3 (bounds) + 4.5 (no moderators)bounded null; small-to-moderate negative effects not excluded
Operator-in-control responds to AI-assistance textResults 4.1 (manipulation evidence)strong
Attribution shifts to AI (common-anchor OR .59/.61)Results 4.4strong
Blame > credit in human+AIResults 4.4suggestive
Attitude moderates AI-only penaltyResults 4.6 "Exploratory analyses" or Discussionexploratory
AI competence penalty only in the relational clipDiscussion, one sentencehint

Stories the data cannot support

  • "AI-controlled robots are trusted less" — trustworthiness did not differ (p = .10–.17 across methods).
  • "Disclosing a disability changes how the operator is judged" — not detected here; effects beyond ~0.5 SD excluded, smaller negative effects not.
  • "Disability status has no effect on how the operator is judged" — also not supported: the study tested one explicit sentence, preceded by stereotype items and followed by an equal-training assurance and competent behaviour.
  • "AI assistance undermines the human operator's standing" — perceptions were equivalent; only attribution shifted.
  • "The disability effect appears in specific tasks or people" — 20 moderator tests, none significant.
  • "People who like AI prefer the AI-controlled robot" — the reversed difference at +1 SD is not significant.
  • "Position of the clip matters for competence" — the position × condition interaction decomposes into nothing.
methods.md · Statistical Methods (draft)

Statistical Methods (draft)

TRIAL STORYLINE — draft text. Revised 2026-09-04 after an independent cross-review. Numbers are taken from numbers_sheet.md and tables.md (generated by paper_numbers.py). The analysis plan described here was fixed before any inferential statistic was computed but was not preregistered; the manuscript must say so.

Participants and analysis sample

Of the 316 people who opened the study on CloudResearch Connect, 300 completed it (1 was screened out for not being able to play video with sound, 15 left before finishing). The analysis sample comprises the 272 completers who passed both quality checks that were built into the questionnaire: an instructed-response attention item on the second clip page ("please select Disagree"; 21 failures) and a four-option comprehension question about the first clip (8 failures, one of them also failing the attention item). Cell sizes in the analysis sample ranged from 36 (AI only) to 41 (HA3). Participants were 18–78 years old (M = 41.2, SD = 13.8), 50% women, and resident in the United States (239), Canada (27), the United Kingdom (5) and Ireland (1); the median completion time was 15.3 min (IQR 12.7–19.7). Two sensitivity samples are reported: all 300 completers, and the analysis sample without the 15 participants who gave the same rating to every item on all three clip pages.

Measures and scoring

After each clip, participants rated on 7-point agreement scales (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree) three statements about OriHime — trustworthy for this task, useful for this task, and willingness to take part in such an interaction — which were averaged into an OriHime evaluation score (Cronbach's α = .79 across clips) and are also reported separately; one statement that the interaction felt genuine rather than like the execution of a program; and two statements about the controller named in the disclosure (warm, competent), plus, in the human conditions only, that the operator was in control of what OriHime said and did. After each clip participants also ranked the actors shown to them (human operator where present, AI system where present, OriHime or its provider, the person in the video) by responsibility for a described negative outcome and by credit for a described positive outcome. After the third clip, performance expectancy (4 items, α = .96) and hedonic motivation (3 items, α = .97) were rated about OriHime in general, followed by how much the participant believed the description of the operator (BEL1), and demographics. Before the disclosure, participants completed the Negative Attitudes towards Robots Scale (10 of the 14 items, three reverse-scored; α = .86), the short General Attitudes towards Artificial Intelligence Scale (positive subscale, 5 items, α = .92; negative subscale, 4 items reverse-scored, α = .85; reported separately as recommended by its authors) and Stereotype Content Model ratings of people with disabilities (competence, 5 items, α = .85; warmth, 4 items, α = .92). All pre-disclosure scales were administered on the same 7-point format as the outcome items.

Analysis plan

The analysis sample, the four primary outcomes (OriHime evaluation, felt genuine, controller warm, controller competent), the primary model and three primary contrasts were fixed before any inferential statistic was computed, but after data collection and after a descriptive pass over the data, and the plan was not registered. We therefore call these analyses pre-specified rather than confirmatory. All other analyses are labelled secondary, sensitivity, robustness or exploratory. Analyses were conducted in Python 3.12 with statsmodels 0.14; code, per-test logs and the complete pairwise tables are provided as supplementary material.

Primary model and contrasts

Clip-level outcomes were analysed with linear mixed-effects models with fixed effects of condition (seven cells), clip (relational, advice, collaboration) and presentation position (first, second, third), and a random intercept for participant, which accounts for the dependence among a participant's three ratings (intraclass correlations .40–.78). Models were fitted by restricted maximum likelihood; omnibus tests of factors and interactions used likelihood-ratio tests on maximum-likelihood fits; contrasts used Wald z tests. Contrasts were linear combinations of the seven cell means with equal cell weights: C1, the six human-involved cells versus the AI-only cell; C2, the three human-operator cells versus the three human-with-AI cells; C3, the four cells in which a disability was disclosed versus the two cells with no mention. C4 (intellectual versus mobility disability) tests the pooling assumed by C3. Within the six human conditions, the control source × profile factorial was tested by likelihood-ratio tests, as were clip × condition and position × condition interactions. All 21 pairwise differences between conditions were also estimated for every outcome and are reported with unadjusted, Holm-adjusted and Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted p values within each outcome's family of 21 comparisons (Supplementary Table S1); the pairwise map was used to describe the pattern of differences, not to select contrasts. Participant-level outcomes (performance expectancy, hedonic motivation, belief) were analysed with ordinary least-squares models with the same contrasts.

Effect sizes are reported as the model estimate in scale points with a 95% confidence interval, and as Cohen's d computed on participant-level means (each participant's mean over the three clips) with the pooled standard deviation of the two groups compared. Primary contrasts are reported with unadjusted p and with Holm adjustment across the four primary outcomes; α = .05, two-sided, throughout.

Assumption checks and robustness

Residuals were left-skewed (skewness −0.35 to −1.06) with ceiling effects (24–36% of ratings at the maximum). Levene's tests showed that between-participant variance was larger in the AI-only condition than in the human conditions (standard-deviation ratios 1.3–1.5; p ≤ .014), so the mixed model's single residual variance understates the uncertainty of contrasts involving that cell. Each primary contrast was therefore re-estimated under seven alternative specifications: the two sensitivity samples; covariate adjustment for centred pre-disclosure scores (GAAIS positive, NARS, SCM warmth) and age, which also addresses chance imbalance across cells in age and AI attitude; Welch's t test and the Mann–Whitney test on participant means; a participant cluster bootstrap (4,000 resamples of participants within cells, percentile intervals); and, for single-item outcomes, proportional-odds GEE models with participant clusters (global-odds-ratio dependence where it converged, otherwise an independence working correlation with cluster-robust standard errors). We describe a contrast as robust when it is significant under every specification and as suggestive when its significance depends on the equal-variance assumption.

Equivalence tests

For the contrasts expected to be null under the storyline (C2, C3, C4) we report two one-sided tests (TOST) on participant-level means with Welch's correction, using equivalence bounds of ±0.35 SD — the smallest standardised difference detectable with 80% power for C2 in this sample — and ±0.50 SD. A difference is reported as bounded within a bound when both one-sided tests reject at α = .05, equivalently when the 90% confidence interval of d lies inside the bound. The bounds are properties of this design's sensitivity, not domain-derived smallest effects of interest, so we describe the results as bounds on the difference rather than as practical equivalence.

Attribution analyses

Whether an actor was ranked first was modelled with generalized estimating equations (binomial family, logit link, exchangeable working correlation, participant clusters) with clip as a covariate; effects are reported as odds ratios. Blame–credit asymmetry was tested at the participant level as the share of clips in which the actor was ranked first for responsibility minus the share for credit (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) and by GEE with question (responsibility versus credit) as a within-participant factor. Because conditions offered three or four actors, the odds of being ranked first fall mechanically when an actor is added and mean ranks are not comparable across conditions. We therefore also report a common-anchor measure — whether the actor was ranked ahead of both actors offered in every condition (OriHime or its provider, and the person in the video) — with the same GEE model, and summarise full rankings by Plackett–Luce worths (minorisation–maximisation estimation), which sum to one within each condition, with participant-bootstrap 95% intervals.

Exploratory analyses

After the primary results were known, eight exploratory blocks (113 tests in total, all listed in Supplementary Table S2 with their p values) examined: moderation of the human-versus-AI contrast by pre-disclosure attitudes (GAAIS, NARS) and by belief in the description; the three components of the OriHime evaluation; moderation of the disclosure contrast by clip, by self-reported contact with people with disabilities and by stereotype content; equivalence tests; and follow-ups of two interaction hints. Interactions were tested by likelihood-ratio tests and conditional effects are reported at ±1 SD of the moderator. For the disclosure contrast we additionally report BIC-approximated Bayes factors computed on participant-level means (the independent units for a between-participant contrast; unit-information prior) and a randomisation test that permutes profile within control source. Belief in the description was measured after the disclosure and is therefore used only for sensitivity analysis, never for exclusion. These analyses are interpreted as hypothesis-generating; one of them (attitude moderation) had been noticed in an earlier descriptive pass of the data and is labelled post hoc.

Missing data

No item was missing other than by design (the operator-control item and the operator/AI rows of the rankings, which were not shown in the conditions lacking that actor) and one participant's age, which excluded that participant from the covariate-adjusted model only.

results.md · Results (draft)

Results (draft)

TRIAL STORYLINE — draft text. Organised in the order of the trial storyline (story.md). Revised 2026-09-04 after an independent cross-review. Evidence levels are tagged in brackets and must survive editing: [pre-specified], [bounded], [secondary], [exploratory]. All numbers come from numbers_sheet.md / tables.md; the primary sample is n = 272 unless stated.

4.1 Preliminary checks

Credibility of the descriptions. Participants believed the description they had been given (BEL1: M = 5.20, SD = 1.52 on the 7-point scale; 76% rated 5 or higher, 17% rated 3 or lower), and belief did not differ between conditions (omnibus p = .451; human-involved versus AI-only Δ = −0.28, p = .302). The three descriptions were therefore equally credible.

Evidence that the control-source text was read. Among participants told that a human operated OriHime, those also told that AI assisted the operator rated the operator as less in control of what OriHime said and did (human 6.14 vs human+AI 5.73; Δ = 0.40 [0.14, 0.66], d = .40, p = .002) [pre-specified]. Disclosing a disability did not change perceived control (Δ = −0.16, p = .245).

Structure of the ratings. Between-participant differences accounted for most of the variance in every clip-level rating (intraclass correlations .40–.78), and the three clips differed strongly: relative to the relational clip, the advice clip raised the OriHime evaluation by 0.36 [0.26, 0.47] and the collaboration clip by 0.20 [0.09, 0.30] scale points (both p < .001); genuineness and controller warmth also rose across presentation positions (p < .001). Omnibus likelihood-ratio tests for the seven-level condition factor were significant for genuineness (p = .004), marginal for warmth (p = .075), and non-significant for the OriHime evaluation (p = .326) and competence (p = .572); the pre-specified contrasts below are the planned decomposition of this factor.

4.2 A human behind the robot makes the interaction feel genuine and the controller warm [pre-specified, C1]

Compared with the six human-involved conditions, the AI-only description lowered perceived genuineness by 0.81 scale points (95% CI 0.35–1.27; d = .62 [.26, .97]; p < .001, Holm-adjusted p = .002; Table 2, Figure 2). This effect was robust: it held in all 300 completers, without straightliners, with adjustment for prior attitudes and age, under Welch's t (p = .017), the Mann–Whitney test (p = .023), a participant cluster bootstrap (p = .011) and an ordinal model (OR = 2.23 [1.17, 4.23], p = .014; Table 3). Every one of the six human-involved cells scored higher than the AI-only cell, and three of these pairwise differences (H1, H3 and HA1 versus A) survived Holm correction within the 21-comparison family.

The controller was also rated as less warm under AI-only control (Δ = 0.50 [0.16, 0.84]; d = .52 [.17, .87]; p = .004, Holm p = .011). This effect held under the bootstrap (p = .031), the ordinal model (OR = 2.35, p = .030) and covariate adjustment (p < .001), but fell just short of significance under Welch's t (p = .052) and the Mann–Whitney test (p = .092); because between-participant variance was 1.3–1.5 times larger in the AI-only cell than in the human cells (Levene p ≤ .014), we regard it as suggestive rather than robust.

The overall OriHime evaluation was lower under AI-only control (Δ = 0.40 [0.06, 0.73]; d = .42 [.07, .77]; p = .020, Holm p = .040), again significant in the model-based analyses but not in the variance-robust ones (Welch p = .069, Mann–Whitney p = .063, bootstrap p = .055). Its components separate the effect: usefulness was lower under AI-only control (Δ = 0.38 [0.08, 0.68], p = .013; bootstrap p = .036; ordinal OR = 1.90, p = .031), willingness to take part was lower with less precision (Δ = 0.56 [0.03, 1.09], p = .039; bootstrap p = .085), whereas trustworthiness did not differ detectably (Δ = 0.25 [−0.05, 0.54], p = .099; bootstrap p = .145). Perceived competence of the controller did not differ (Δ = 0.22 [−0.07, 0.52]; d = .27; p = .135).

The pattern across the full pairwise map was the same for all four primary outcomes (Figure 1; Supplementary Table S1): of the 84 pairwise comparisons, the 10 with unadjusted p < .05 all contrasted a human-involved cell with the AI-only cell, and none of the 60 comparisons among the six human-involved cells reached p < .05. At the level of control source, both the human and the human+AI conditions exceeded the AI-only condition on genuineness (d = .64 and .53; p < .001 and .003) and warmth (d = .46 and .51; p = .006 and .007). Clip did not moderate the human-versus-AI contrast (likelihood-ratio tests, p ≥ .13 for the primary outcomes; Figure 3); within each clip the genuineness difference was significant (p ≤ .047).

4.3 What does not change: AI assistance, and who the operator is [pre-specified C2–C4, reported as bounds]

Human versus human with AI assistance. Participants told that AI assisted the operator gave the same ratings as those told that the operator worked alone: OriHime evaluation d = −.08 [−.34, .17] (p = .539), genuineness d = .12 (p = .377), warmth d = .02 (p = .912), competence d = −.17 (p = .209), performance expectancy d = −.17 (p = .209), hedonic motivation d = −.04 (p = .747). Equivalence tests with bounds of ±0.35 SD rejected differences of that size for the OriHime evaluation (p = .020), genuineness (p = .047), warmth (p = .006) and hedonic motivation (p = .009), and with bounds of ±0.50 SD for every outcome (p ≤ .006; Table 4). The difference between human and human+AI operation was thus bounded within half a standard deviation on all perception measures, and within a third of a standard deviation on most, even though the AI-assistance text had measurably reduced perceived operator control (4.1). These bounds are the design's smallest detectable effects rather than domain-derived smallest effects of interest, so we describe the result as a bounded difference rather than as practical equivalence.

Explicit disclosure of the operator's disability. Within the six human-operator conditions, explicitly disclosing an intellectual or mobility-related disability, compared with omitting disability information, did not produce statistically detectable average differences in the four primary outcomes (two-sided p ≥ .112; Table 2). All unadjusted point estimates were negative: OriHime evaluation d = −.10 (p = .491), genuineness d = −.24 [−.51, .03] (p = .112), warmth d = −.25 [−.52, .03] (p = .114), competence d = −.14 (p = .342), operator in control d = −.16 (p = .245), performance expectancy d = −.13 (p = .361), hedonic motivation d = −.26 (p = .076). For genuineness and warmth, participant-mean (HC3), cluster-bootstrap and randomisation analyses gave p = .06–.09, so these outcomes remain compatible with small-to-moderate negative effects as well as with zero; with 159 disclosed and 77 no-mention participants the design detects d ≥ .39 with 80% power and has 41% power at d = .24. The two nearest-to-significant estimates shrank after adjustment for prior attitudes and age (genuineness Δ = −0.10, p = .570; warmth Δ = −0.18, p = .166); the no-mention cells were, by chance, older (46.1 vs 38.8 years) and somewhat more AI-positive, but the adjustment is a post hoc sensitivity analysis and is reported alongside, not instead of, the unadjusted estimates. TOST bounded the disclosure difference within ±0.35 SD for the OriHime evaluation (p = .040) and within ±0.50 SD for genuineness, warmth, competence, performance expectancy and hedonic motivation (p ≤ .032; Table 4); BIC-approximated Bayes factors on participant-level means favoured the null by 11.7 (OriHime evaluation), 9.2 (competence), 7.6 (operator in control), 3.5 (genuineness) and 3.2 (warmth) to one. The data therefore rule out large effects more clearly than small-to-moderate negative ones. Because the manipulation was a single sentence, preceded by stereotype items about people with disabilities and followed by an equal-training assurance and competent behaviour, and because disability-specific uptake was not measured (participants in the disclosure cells spent 5.5 s longer on the disclosure page, p = .023, consistent with reading the sentence, but recall and belief of the disability content were not assessed), this result is a null average effect of explicit disclosure in this framing, not evidence that disability status in general has no effect. The two types of disability did not differ from each other on any outcome (|d| ≤ .17; bounded within ±0.35 SD for all outcomes except genuineness), which supports pooling them. Disclosure did not interact with control source (likelihood-ratio p ≥ .18) or with clip (p ≥ .068), and did not depend on participants' contact with people with disabilities (p ≥ .36) or on their stereotype ratings of people with disabilities (p ≥ .27; 20 moderator tests, none significant) [exploratory]. Disclosure also left attribution unchanged (below).

4.4 AI involvement moves responsibility and credit away from the operator [pre-specified, RQ4]

When a human operated OriHime without AI, participants ranked the operator first for responsibility in 72% of clips and first for credit in 71%. Adding AI assistance lowered the odds of ranking the operator first (responsibility: 55%, OR = 0.47 [0.31, 0.73], p = .001; credit: 51%, OR = 0.42 [0.27, 0.64], p < .001; Table 5). Because the human+AI condition offered four actors rather than three, part of this drop is mechanical; anchored on the two actors offered in every condition, the operator was ranked ahead of both OriHime's provider and the person in the video in 72.3% of rankings under human control and 60.7% under human+AI control for responsibility (OR = 0.59 [0.36, 0.93], p = .022), and 71.2% vs 60.2% for credit (OR = 0.61, p = .032; Table 7), so the reallocation is real but smaller than the raw odds ratios suggest. The lost share went to the AI: Plackett–Luce worths (Table 6, Figure 4) fell from .68 [.62, .75] for the operator working alone to .45 [.38, .53] with AI assistance, while the AI received .28 [.25, .32] and the shares of OriHime's provider (.19 → .18) and of the person in the video (.13 → .09) did not rise. When the operator was ranked first in the human+AI condition, the AI was ranked second in 64–67% of rankings. With no human present, the AI was ranked first in 57% (responsibility) and 60% (credit) of clips (OR versus human+AI ≈ 7.8, p < .001), with a worth of .55 [.43, .66]; the remainder went mostly to OriHime's provider (.30). On the common anchor, however, the AI's standing relative to the provider and the interlocutor was similar with and without a human (ranked ahead of both in 52% vs 57% of rankings for responsibility, OR = 1.24, p = .471; 49% vs 60% for credit, OR = 1.60, p = .139), so the large raw odds ratio mainly reflects the absence of the human operator from the list rather than a re-evaluation of the AI. Disclosing the operator's disability did not change the odds of the operator being ranked first (responsibility OR = 0.89 [0.57, 1.40], p = .624; credit OR = 0.80 [0.51, 1.25], p = .322).

In the human+AI condition, the operator was slightly more often ranked first for responsibility than for credit (55.4% vs 50.6% of clips per participant, +4.8 points; Wilcoxon p = .024; GEE OR = 1.21, p = .032; no interaction with clip, p = .89) [secondary]. No such asymmetry appeared for the operator working alone (+1.1 points, p = .536) or for the AI in the AI-only condition (−2.8 points, p = .433).

4.5 General acceptance did not depend on condition [secondary]

Performance expectancy (omnibus p = .610) and hedonic motivation (p = .395) did not differ across the seven conditions, and no pre-specified contrast reached significance (Table 2). A marginal difference in hedonic motivation between the disclosure and no-mention cells (Δ = −0.40 [−0.84, 0.04], p = .076) was traced to a single cell (HA1, M = 5.61 versus 4.85–5.16 in the other five human cells) and disappeared after covariate adjustment (Δ = −0.21, p = .263); we do not interpret it.

4.6 Exploratory analyses [exploratory; 113 tests, all listed in Supplementary Table S2]

Who pays the AI-only penalty. Participants' prior attitude to AI (GAAIS positive subscale, measured before the disclosure) moderated the human-versus-AI contrast. Ratings rose more steeply with positive attitude in the AI-only condition than in the human-involved conditions (slopes per scale point .50 vs .28 for the OriHime evaluation, interaction p = .019; .38 vs .10 for competence, p = .003; .48 vs .23 for genuineness, p = .083; .28 vs .10 for warmth, p = .093; Figure 5). Among participants one SD below the mean attitude, the AI-only penalty was 0.44 (OriHime evaluation, p = .014), 0.91 (genuineness, p < .001), 0.62 (warmth, p = .003) and 0.42 scale points (competence, p = .015); among participants one SD above the mean, no difference was significant (−0.20 to +0.20; p ≥ .10). The human+AI slope (.30) matched the human slope (.26): attitude-dependence was triggered by the absence of a human, not by the presence of AI. This pattern had been noticed in a descriptive pass before the formal analysis and is reported as post hoc. Restricting the sample to participants who believed the description (n = 206) left the primary contrast unchanged (genuineness Δ = 0.83, p = .001; warmth Δ = 0.52, p = .006; OriHime evaluation Δ = 0.40, p = .025).

A competence penalty confined to the relational clip. The competence rating showed the only hint of a clip-specific effect: the AI-only penalty was larger in the relational clip than in the two task clips (interaction contrast 0.33, p = .037), although within the relational clip alone the difference was not significant (ordinal OR = 1.78 [0.88, 3.58], p = .108). A position × condition interaction for competence (p = .012) did not decompose into any interpretable component (human × position p = .514; control source × position p = .617) and is treated as noise.

Bookkeeping. Of the 113 exploratory tests, 37 reached p < .05; 11 of these are equivalence tests (where p < .05 indicates equivalence) and 13 are mean-rank comparisons that are not interpretable across conditions offering different numbers of actors. Of the remaining 79 tests, 13 reached p < .05 against about 4 expected by chance; they cluster in the attitude-moderation block and in the sample restrictions that reproduce the primary contrast.

  • Table S2. Log of the 113 exploratory tests with block, estimate and p (results/phase14_test_log.csv).
  • Table S3. Robustness of the primary contrasts across specifications (results/robustness.csv, results/bootstrap_contrasts.csv).
limitations.md · Limitations and reviewer-facing rationale (draft)

Limitations (draft) and reviewer-facing methodological rationale

TRIAL STORYLINE — draft text. Revised 2026-09-04 after an independent cross-review.

Limitations

No direct manipulation check of control source. The questionnaire did not ask participants to restate who controlled OriHime. Three indirect indicators are available: the three descriptions were believed to the same degree (76% of the analysis sample rated belief ≥ 5 of 7; no condition differences, p = .45), participants told that AI assisted the operator rated the operator as less in control (d = .40, p = .002), and participants in the AI-only condition ranked the AI first for responsibility and credit in 57–60% of clips, against 15–16% when a human was also present. These show that the text was read and believed, not that it produced the intended mental model in every participant.

Unequal precision across conditions. The design allocated one cell to AI-only control and six to human control, so contrasts involving the AI-only cell rest on 36 participants against 236. With 80% power the design detects a human-versus-AI difference of about d = .50 in the analysis sample, and a disclosure difference of about d = .39; smaller differences — for example in competence (d = .27) — cannot be excluded. Between-participant variance was also larger in the AI-only cell, which is why the warmth and usefulness effects are reported as suggestive rather than robust.

Task type is confounded with clip length. The three clips run 70, 105 and 115 s and differ in content, so clip effects — which were large — are treated as nuisance terms, and the tentative observation that the AI competence penalty was confined to the relational clip is reported only as a hint.

Single-item measures and ceiling effects. Genuineness, warmth, competence and operator control were single items with 24–36% of ratings at the scale maximum. Ordinal robustness models agree with the linear models for the main contrast, but the single items limit reliability and the ceiling compresses differences among the human conditions.

The disclosure was minimal, and the material worked against it. The operator's disability was stated in one sentence on one page, before any clip, and was never repeated or depicted. Three features of the material would each be expected to weaken a label effect: all participants had just answered nine stereotype items about people with disabilities, so disability was salient in every cell including the no-mention control; the disability sentence was immediately followed by the assurance that all operators complete the same training and meet the same standard, which directly counters a competence stereotype; and the clips then showed fluent, competent performance (73% of competence ratings in the human conditions were 6 or 7). Uptake of the disability sentence specifically was not measured: the disclosure cells spent 5.5 s longer on the page, consistent with reading it, but the belief item asked about the description as a whole and there was no recall check. The null therefore applies to this minimal, textual form of disclosure in this framing and should not be generalised to visible or repeated cues or read as evidence that disability status has no effect. The control condition said nothing about disability rather than stating its absence, by design; the contrast is therefore explicit disclosure versus omission, not disability versus no disability.

Sample and setting. Participants were an English-speaking online panel, mostly in the United States, watching pre-recorded clips of one robot in one workplace; the videos were identical across conditions, which is the study's strength for isolating prior attribution but limits ecological validity.

Analysis plan not preregistered. The primary sample, outcomes, model and contrasts were fixed before inferential testing but after data collection and a descriptive pass, and were not registered externally, so we call them pre-specified rather than confirmatory. The exploratory analyses are numerous (113 tests); one of them had been seen in an earlier descriptive pass. All exploratory results are reported in full and none is treated as confirmatory.

Reviewer-facing rationale

Why a linear mixed model rather than ANOVA on participant means? Each participant rated three clips; the mixed model uses all 816 ratings while accounting for their dependence through a random intercept (ICC .40–.78), adjusts for clip and position, and allows clip × condition interactions to be tested. Analyses on participant means (Welch t, Mann–Whitney) are reported as robustness checks and, for the main contrast, agree in direction and mostly in significance.

*Why report unadjusted pairwise p values at all?* The 21 pairwise differences per outcome were computed to display the full pattern of condition differences (all significant differences among the primary outcomes involve the AI-only cell; none separates any two human cells), not to select findings. They are presented with Holm and Benjamini–Hochberg adjustments in the supplement, and inference rests on the three pre-specified contrasts.

Why equal-weight cell means in the contrasts? Cells differ in size only through random loss (36–41); equal weighting makes C1–C4 estimate the design's intended comparisons rather than a mixture weighted by drop-out.

Why is the AI-only condition one cell? Operator profile is undefined when no operator exists; the design is 3 × 2 plus one reference cell, not 3 × 3. This is why C1 compares six cells against one and why the reference cell has lower precision.

Why equivalence tests, and why not call the results equivalent? A non-significant difference does not show similarity. TOST with pre-stated bounds (±0.35 SD, the design's smallest detectable effect for C2; ±0.50 SD) lets us state within what range the human-versus-human+AI and disclosure effects lie. Because the bounds come from the design's sensitivity rather than from a domain-derived smallest effect of interest, we report them as bounds on the difference and avoid the word equivalent without the bound attached.

Why report the attribution shift with a common anchor? The human+AI condition offered one more actor to rank, so the odds of ranking the operator first fall even if beliefs are unchanged. Anchored on the two actors offered everywhere, the operator was still ranked ahead of both less often under human+AI control (OR .59 for responsibility, .61 for credit), so the shift is not only a menu effect, but the raw odds ratios overstate it.

Is the genuineness effect a demand artefact? The genuineness item ("felt genuine, rather than like the execution of a program") is worded close to the AI-only description ("controlled entirely by an AI system"), so part of its large effect may reflect consistency with the description rather than perception. The warmth and usefulness effects, whose wording is not tied to the manipulation, and the equal belief ratings across conditions argue against a purely demand-driven account, but the item cannot be treated as independent of the manipulation's wording.

Why compute Bayes factors on participant means? Disclosure is a between-participant variable; the 708 clip ratings are not 708 independent pieces of evidence about it. BIC-approximated Bayes factors on the 236 participant means favour the null by 3–12 to one depending on the outcome, moderate rather than strong evidence, and depend on the unit-information prior implicit in the BIC approximation.

Why not exclude participants who disbelieved the description? Belief was measured after the clips and after all outcome items; disbelief may itself be a reaction to the condition (a participant told "AI only" who found the interaction genuine may doubt the description). Excluding on a post-treatment variable would condition on an outcome. Belief is used for sensitivity analysis: restricting to believers (n = 206) leaves the main contrast unchanged.

How is heteroscedasticity handled? Levene's tests indicated larger variance in the AI-only cell. Contrasts involving that cell are re-estimated with Welch's t, the Mann–Whitney test and a participant cluster bootstrap, none of which assumes equal variances; the genuineness effect survives all of them, the warmth and usefulness effects survive most.

Why Plackett–Luce for the rankings? Conditions offered three or four actors, so mean ranks are not comparable across conditions; the share ranked first (GEE) and Plackett–Luce worths (normalised within condition) are.

How many tests were run? 225 pairwise comparisons (supplement), 12 primary contrast tests (Holm within contrast), 6 secondary contrasts per outcome, 45 interaction tests, and 113 exploratory tests, all logged. Expected false positives at α = .05 are stated next to each family.

Reproducibility

analysis/README.md describes the pipeline; run_all.sh re-runs everything from the raw export to the workbook (about 5 minutes). Supplementary tables S1 (225 pairwise comparisons) and S2 (113 exploratory tests) are results/pairwise_all.csv and results/phase14_test_log.csv. The code is on the branch study1-analysis.

Appendix A · Supplementary sweep of the disability factor

Supplementary sweep of the disability factor

Corrections after the cross-review

On 2026-09-04 an independent cross-review (analysis/study1-20260902-cross-review/workbook_cross_review.html) recomputed every number in this appendix — all matched — but found the narration too strong. The appendix has been revised accordingly; corrected points are marked “cross-review” in each subsection. Key points: Bayes factors are now computed on participant units; “was read” and “was believed” are stated separately; D1 and D2 cannot exclude the label being overridden within the first clip; the conclusion is limited to “the incremental effect of an explicit one-sentence disclosure”; the stereotype pre-measure, the equal-training assurance and the competent clips all weaken a label and count as boundary conditions.

Answers to the four questions

Q1Is there really nothing left to find? In these data and this material, no significant effect can be found. Eight further analyses targeted the disability factor: 31 tests, 3 with p < .05 against 1.6 expected by chance, and none of the 3 is “disclosure has an effect”. Bayes factors on participant units: OH 11.7, competence 9.2, performance expectancy 9.6, operator control 7.6 favour the null; genuineness 3.5 and warmth 3.2 are only weak-to-moderate; hedonic motivation 2.8. All four primary point estimates are negative, genuineness and warmth d ≈ −.24 with 95% intervals reaching −.5 and participant-level p .06–.09. The correct statement: not detected, large effects excluded, small-to-moderate negative effects not excluded. (Corrected after the 2026-09-04 cross-review: the earlier “20 to 1 for the null” used the wrong information unit.)

Q2What would more participants do to the p-values? If the effect size stays the same, z grows with the square root of the sample size. Genuineness and warmth currently have d ≈ −.24, p .11: doubling the human cells would bring p to about .025; the smallest effect this design detects reliably for C3 is d = .39, power at d = .24 is only 41%, and 80% power would need about 610 people against the current 236. Three reasons not to do it: after adding pre-measure covariates the estimates shrink to −.10 and −.18, so part of the −.24 may come from the no-mention group happening to be older (46.1 vs 38.8 years) and more AI-positive — though that is a post hoc sensitivity analysis and cannot adjudicate alone; deciding to add people after seeing p = .11 is “optional stopping”, which inflates the false-positive rate and must be declared; and even if significant, 0.3 points on a 7-point scale cannot carry a story. If it must be tested, open a preregistered replication cell with a stronger disclosure and a fixed sample size and analysis.

Q3Could the clips be non-neutral? The suspicion is reasonable: competence ratings in the human conditions average 5.86 and 73% are ≥ 6; participants watched a fluent, competent operator, which leaves the “intellectual disability” label little room to act. Two more features of the material weaken the label: nine stereotype items about people with disabilities were answered before the disclosure, and the disclosure sentence was followed immediately by the assurance that all operators complete the same training and meet the same standard. The data can say only so much: there is evidence the sentence was read (the disclosure cells dwelt 5.5 s longer on the page, p .023, consistent with reading one sentence), but whether it was remembered or believed was not measured directly — BEL1 asks about the whole description; after the first clip there is no difference between disclosure and no mention (D2), but with no pre-clip baseline the label could have acted and been overridden by behavioural evidence within the first clip, so “the clip overrides the label” is neither supported nor excluded. The default impression the clips give can be tested directly in Study 2: a new sample with no description answers “does this person have a disability”; if most say “no” or “can't tell”, the clips carry a “no disability” signal that conflicts with the H2/H3 descriptions — but that cannot retroactively show that Study 1's participants read or believed the sentence.

Q4Can disability still open the story? Yes, but only as a “bounded null” story: open with OriHime being operated by people with disabilities, ask “does knowing the operator has a disability change how the interaction is judged”, and answer “not detectably in this material: effects beyond half an SD are excluded, participant-unit Bayes factors of 3–12 favour the null, evaluations and attribution show no detectable change, and the only thing that changed evaluations was whether a human was present at all”. The price is answering three objections head-on: the one-sentence disclosure is weak, the competence assurance that follows it neutralises the stereotype, and whether the label was believed was not measured. Available answers are the dwell time, Study 2's default impression and the TOST bounds, with visible or repeated disclosure and a disability-specific recall item listed as future work. The data support neither “disclosure changed evaluations” nor the general claim “disability status itself has no effect”.

Checklist of tests

Already tested before this sweep: the pooled contrast C3 and its parts C4, C5a, C5b (all outcomes); control source × profile interaction; profile × clip; three moderators (contact frequency, SCM warmth, SCM competence); attribution rankings; PE, HM, BEL1; equivalence tests. None significant. The eight new analyses below add 31 tests, 3 with p < .05 against about 1.6 expected.

BlockTestsp < .05
D1 disclosure × position52

D3 warmth − competence10
D4 attribution within HA/H140

D6 dwell time31
Total313

D1 · Disclosure effect × presentation position

Why it is legitimate: if fluent, competent behaviour in the clips overrides the “has a disability” label, the disclosure effect should be largest on the first clip and fade afterwards. Result: after the first clip the disclosure effect is near zero (differences of −0.03 to −0.15 on the five outcomes); on the third clip a consistent −0.26 to −0.37 appears (p .03–.056), with significant interactions on OH (p = .026) and CR2 (p = .033).

Reading: the no-mention group's ratings rise with position (the general position effect), the disclosure group's do not. This is not “the label washed out by the clips”; it looks more like “the label's influence accumulating”, or simply noise: it is post hoc, 2 of 5 interactions are significant, and the outcomes are correlated, so it is a lead, not a finding. It cannot refute “fast override”: the first measurement comes after 70–115 s of video, there is no post-disclosure, pre-clip baseline, and the label may have acted and been overridden within the first clip (pointed out by the 2026-09-04 cross-review).

D2 · First clip only

Right after reading the description and watching one clip, disclosure and no-mention ratings are almost identical (d between −.04 and −.10, p ≥ .41). That is, no detectable difference after the first clip; with no pre-clip measurement, this does not mean the label never acted immediately.

The stereotype content model predicts a paternalistic “high warmth, low competence” pattern for disability, i.e. a wider warmth-minus-competence gap after disclosure. The gap actually narrows slightly (−0.10, p = .18; intellectual disability −0.13, p = .076): no paternalistic pattern.

D5 · Belief by profile

The two intellectual-disability cells average BEL1 4.96 against 5.27 in the other human cells (p = .17); H2 is lowest at 4.85 with 23% disbelievers against 15% in H1. Directionally, “a human operator with an intellectual disability” is the hardest of the six descriptions to believe, but the difference is not significant.

D6 · Dwell time on the disclosure page

Participants told of a disability spent a median 45.7 s on the description page against 40.2 s for no mention (Mann–Whitney p = .023; medians 57 and 52 s in HA2 and HA3). There is evidence the extra sentence was read: 5.5 s matches the reading time of a sentence of a dozen words. Whether it was remembered or believed was not measured directly; BEL1 asks about the whole description. Dwell time does not moderate the disclosure effect (p ≥ .49). This can go in the paper to answer “was it even read”, not “was it believed”.

BF01 is the evidence for “no disclosure effect” relative to “some effect”. Corrected after the 2026-09-04 cross-review: disability is a between-participant variable, so the independent information units are the 236 participants, not the 708 clip rows; the earlier clip-row BIC overstated the evidence by about 1.7×. Recomputed on participant means: OH 11.7 is strong, CR2 9.2, PE 9.6 and CR3 7.6 moderate, AU1 3.5 and CR1 3.2 weak-to-moderate, HM 2.8 weak. All favour the null, but for genuineness and warmth the evidence is not enough to write “the data support no effect”; and the BIC approximation depends on a unit-information prior, which the paper must state.

D8 · Sample-size projections

How p changes with sample size: if the effect size stays the same, z scales with √(multiplier). AU1 and CR1 currently have d ≈ −.24: adding as many people again to the human cells (236 → 472) would bring p to about .025, and 610 people would give 80% power to detect d = .24. Three things make this route unattractive: after covariate adjustment the estimates shrink to −.10 and −.18, so part of the −.24 is the no-mention group being older and more AI-positive by chance; deciding to add people after seeing p = .11 and testing again is “optional stopping”, which inflates the false-positive rate, must be declared in the paper and will be questioned by reviewers; and even if significant, a 0.3-point difference on a 7-point scale is small and cannot carry the story. If more data are collected, the right way is a separate preregistered replication cell with a stronger disclosure (repeated, visible cues), not topping up the current cells.
