Neutrality of the clips

  • The operator in the clips performs fluently; competence ratings in the human conditions average 5.86 with 72% of ratings ≥ 6. Participants saw competent performance, which does compress the room for an “intellectual disability” label to act. But this is part of the design: every condition watches the same clips, which is what isolates the effect as prior attribution.
  • What the data can say: there is evidence the label was read (D6), but remembering and believing were not measured directly; no difference after the first clip (D2), but with no pre-clip baseline a fast override cannot be excluded (D1). So “the clip overrides the label” is neither directly supported nor excluded in these data; the more accurate statement is “given observed competent performance, a one-off textual disclosure does not change evaluations”.
  • The data that can test the clips' neutrality directly are Study 2's. Study 2 asks a new sample, with no description, “who is controlling” and “does the person have a disability”. If most answer “no disability” or “can't tell”, the clips carry a “no disability” signal that conflicts with the H2/H3 descriptions, the strongest available explanation of this study's null; if answers are spread out, the clips are neutral and the null is more likely genuine. This step is far cheaper than adding participants.

Feasibility of opening the story with disability

Yes, but only as a bounded story: open with OriHime being operated by people with disabilities, ask “does knowing the operator has a disability change how people judge the interaction”, and answer “not detectably in this material: there is evidence the label was read, evaluations and attribution show no detectable change (effects beyond half an SD excluded, participant-unit BF01 3–12), and the only thing that changed evaluations was whether a human was present”. This is a conclusion with positive implications for inclusive remote work. Its price is facing the objection that a one-sentence disclosure is too weak — answered with D6, Study 2 and the TOST bounds — while acknowledging that BEL1 is not disability-specific and that the “same training” assurance in the material weakens the label, and listing visible or repeated disclosure and a disability-specific recall item as future work. What the data do not support is any claim that “disclosing a disability changed evaluations”.

Appendix B · Study 2 plan (draft, 2026-09-04)

Study 2 plan

Current design

A fresh sample, no disclosure at all. Page one explains that OriHime can be controlled in three ways (human, human + AI assistance, AI only) without saying which applies. The three clips are the same as in Study 1, in the six balanced orders. After each clip, three items: IMP, an open description (“what does the interaction look like to you”, at least 10 characters); after a reminder of the three methods, WHO (human / human + AI / AI / can't tell); DIS (if a person is involved, does that person have a disability: yes / no / can't tell / I don't think a person is involved). No demographics, attitudes, belief or evaluation items, and no attention check. Study 1 participants are refused by the server.

Questions Study 2 can answer

QuestionOutcomeAnalysisMeaning for Study 1
S2-Q1 Without disclosure, who do viewers assume is in controlWHO, per clipoption shares with Wilson intervals; departure from uniform across the three methods; share of “can't tell”if Study 1's “AI only” description conflicts with viewers' default impression, the AI-condition penalty contains a “label vs impression conflict” component
S2-Q2 Without disclosure, do viewers infer a disabilityDIS, per clip (among WHO answers that include a person)shares of yes / no / can't tell; whether “no” is the majoritya direct test of “the clips carry a no-disability signal”. “No” majority → Study 1's disclosure conflicted with observation; “can't tell” majority → the clips are neutral and Study 1's null is more likely genuine
S2-Q3 Does the inference vary by clip typeWHO, DIS × clipwithin-person comparisons (Cochran's Q / multinomial GEE), position and order effectsif the chat clip reads as human and the task clips as AI, this matches Study 1's lead that “the AI competence penalty appears only in the chat clip”
S2-Q4 Which cues do viewers useIMP open descriptions; reasons for WHO (if added)coding: speech fluency, response latency, content, gestures, reference terms (it / she / the operator), mentions of AI or disability; double-coder agreementexplains Study 1's mechanism: which cues “genuineness” hangs on
S2-Q5 Is a person's judgement consistent across the three clipswithin-person consistency of WHOshare giving the same answer on all three; anchoring on the first clip by orderdistinguishes “a person's prior” from “clip-driven inference”
S2-Q6 Internal consistency checkWHO = AI but DIS ≠ “no person involved”share of contradictory answers as a quality indicator—

Link to Study 1

  • Study 1 measured what an imposed attribution changes; Study 2 measures what the spontaneous attribution is. Only together can they say whether a disclosure failed (disability) or worked (AI only) because it agreed with or conflicted with viewers' own impression.
  • The DIS result decides how Study 1's disability null is written. “No” majority: “a one-sentence label overridden by observed competent performance”. “Can't tell” majority: “even with nothing to contradict it, the label does not change evaluations”.
  • The WHO result decides how deep the “AI-only penalty” interpretation can go. If most assume a human, part of A's penalty comes from “told one thing, saw another”; if “can't tell” dominates, the penalty is the label itself.

Recommended changes before launch (by value; each needs a code change and a deploy; item ids freeze once collection starts)

  1. Confidence in WHO (1 item per clip): “how confident are you in this judgement”, 1–7. Separates confident judgements from guesses and allows weighted analyses. Lowest cost, highest value.
  2. Evaluation items comparable with Study 1 (2 per clip): AU1 “this interaction felt genuine, rather than like the execution of a program” and OH2 “OriHime was useful for this task”. Placed after IMP and before the reminder of the three methods, so the option list does not steer them. With these, “do people who spontaneously judge the controller to be an AI also find it less genuine” can be tested, replicating Study 1's strongest finding without disclosure.
  3. Follow-up to DIS (optional, not required): if “yes”, ask “what kind of disability” (open); shows whether “intellectual disability” is ever inferred spontaneously (it was the least believed description in Study 1).
  4. Reason for WHO (optional short answer): “what made you think so?” collects cues more directly than IMP.
  5. Background block at the end: age, gender, AI-use frequency, contact with people with disabilities, plus the 5 GAAIS positive items. Study 1 found attitude moderating the AI-only penalty; in Study 2 attitude probably predicts the tendency to infer AI. At the end, it cannot affect the judgements.
  6. Quality control: raise the IMP minimum from 10 to 30 characters; add an instructed-response attention check on the second clip (as in Study 1), otherwise quality can only be judged from text quality and playback telemetry.
  7. One closing item (optional): “was OriHime controlled the same way in all three clips”, helps interpret within-person consistency.

Sample size

The core quantities are option shares per clip. At n = 200 a share's 95% interval is about ±7 points, at n = 300 about ±5.5, at n = 385 about ±5. Within-person comparisons between clips detect a 10-point difference reliably at n = 200. Recommendation: 250–300 people, 10–15 minutes each, far cheaper than topping up Study 1.

Scenario analysis: non-neutral clips

Premise: non-neutrality does not invalidate Study 1's comparisons. The clips are a constant across conditions, and randomisation guarantees an unbiased estimate of condition differences for these clips. What non-neutrality changes is the mechanism (does a label fill a vacuum or conflict with an impression), the meaning of the nulls, and the range of generalisation. The scenarios Study 2 might produce are worked through below.

Dimension one: whom most viewers assume to be in control (WHO)

ScenarioWhich Study 1 descriptions match the defaultReading of the AI-only penalty (C1)Reading of H = HA (C2)Write-up and risk
W1 Majority “human”H, HA match; A conflictspenalty = label content + conflict with the impression, inseparable within Study 1. Side evidence favours label content: A's belief equals the other groups'; the penalty varies with attitude to AI, whereas pure conflict should hit everyoneboth match the default; the label has no room to add, so equivalence is partly a ceiling“even when the clips read as human-controlled by default, being told AI-only still lowers genuineness”, i.e. the label overrides the impression. The Discussion must acknowledge the conflict component
W2 Majority “AI”A matches; H, HA conflictthe same difference becomes a “human label bonus”; the title holds literallyboth conflict with the same effect, so what matters is “a human is present”, not “purely human”most favourable for the paper. H2 and H3 stack a disability label on top of an AI default, a double conflict, so the disability null needs one more sentence
W3 Majority “human + AI”HA matches; H and A deviate in opposite directionsdeviating towards “pure AI” costsdeviating towards “pure human” adds nothing; an asymmetric effect“AI assistance is the default assumption; only removing the human costs”
W4 Majority “can't tell” or a flat distributionnothing conflictsa pure label effect, the cleanest casea pure label effectall conclusions as currently written; A's larger variance attributed to attitude, not conflict
W5 Varies by clipdiffers per clipA's penalty should be largest where the default is most “human”. In Study 1 the OH penalty is largest in the chat clip (d .51 vs .34, .25), interaction p .13: direction matches, evidence weakas aboveclip differences could be promoted from “nuisance” to “moderation by the default impression”, but only with a significant interaction

Dimension two: whether most viewers assume a disability (DIS)

ScenarioWhat the control cells H1, HA1 actually areMeaning of the disability null (C3)Write-up and risk
Da Majority “no”default: no disabilityC3 is a clean “told yes vs assumed no” contrast. The null means a one-sentence label did not change evaluations even against observation; believed but not absorbed into the evaluation“observation overrides a one-sentence label”. Limitation: does not generalise to a visible disability
Db Majority “yes”a disability is already assumedthe worst case. Both groups assume a disability, C3 becomes “told vs assumed”, and the null says nothing about a disability label; Study 1 has no “assumed no disability” cell to comparethe disability part can only be written as “explicit disclosure has no incremental effect”. A real test needs a new condition: clips with a different operator, or an explicit “no disability” description (deliberately avoided in the design)
Dc Majority “can't tell”a genuine blankthe label is the only source of information; the null is the strongest “the label does not matter”most favourable for a disability-equivalence story
Dd Split (e.g. 40 / 40 / 20)heterogeneousStudy 1's null is an average over heterogeneous effects. The two studies are different samples and cannot be linked at the individual level, only at the clip levelneeds the WHO and DIS confidence items to judge how strong the default is
De Depends on WHOthose who think AI answer “no person involved”analysis restricted to answers that include a person (already in the plan)also yields the share who think a person is involved

Combinations

  • Best: W4 plus Dc, both near neutral, all conclusions as currently written.
  • Most favourable for the title: W2 plus Da or Dc, the human label is a bonus and the disability label does not change evaluations.
  • Most rewriting: Db. The disability null loses its meaning, is downgraded to “explicit disclosure has no incremental effect”, and a new condition becomes future work.
  • Most to defend in the Discussion: W1 plus Da, the AI-only penalty is mixed with conflict, argued with the two side findings “equal belief” and “attitude moderation”.

Decision rules fixed in advance

  • “Majority”: share > 50% with the lower bound of the 95% interval > 50%.
  • “Neutral”: no option above 40%, or “can't tell” ≥ 40%.
  • “Varies by clip”: Cochran's Q p < .05 and at least one clip with a different majority option.
  • Confidence items separate “weak default” from “strong default”; a weak default is treated as near neutral.
  • When Study 2 data arrive, first classify the scenario by these rules, then revise Study 1's write-up; the classification goes into the Analysis Log.

Analysis plan (fixed before the data arrive)

  • Primary: shares of WHO and DIS per clip with Wilson intervals; DIS computed among answers that include a person, with the share of “I don't think a person is involved” reported separately.
  • Clip differences: Cochran's Q (after dichotomising) and multinomial GEE logit (participant clusters), controlling for presentation position.
  • Within-person consistency: share with the same WHO on all three clips against the expectation under random answering; the first answer predicting the next two.
  • Open descriptions: build a cue coding scheme first (voice, latency, fluency, content relevance, gestures, reference terms, AI words, disability words); two coders code 20% independently for agreement; the rest may be model-assisted and then checked; cue rates compared by WHO group.
  • Link to Study 1: if AU1/OH2 are added, compare AU1 by WHO (spontaneous AI vs human) alongside Study 1's C1 effect size.
  • Quality: share of contradictory answers, IMP length, playback telemetry; exclusion rules stated in advance.

Changes to the plan

  • 2026-09-04 · Added the pooled contrast C3 “disability disclosed vs no mention” and C4 “intellectual vs mobility”. Reason: research question (you asked whether any disclosure has an effect). Added before any p-value was seen, so it counts as a primary contrast.
  • 2026-09-04 · Added the participant bootstrap as a robustness check. Reason: model assumption — Levene's test found clearly larger variance in A, so the primary model's equal-variance assumption fails and contrasts involving A need a check that does not depend on it.
  • 2026-09-04 · Ordinal GEE for CR1, CR2, OH1–3 switched to an independence working correlation with robust standard errors. Reason: numerical — the global-odds-ratio structure did not converge on these items.
  • 2026-09-04 · BEL1 renamed from “manipulation check” to “credibility check”. Reason: research logic — it shows the description was believed, not that it changed perception; the latter is evidenced by CR3.
  • 2026-09-04 · No top-up of cell A. Reason: time. Consequence: the precision of contrasts involving A is fixed at a detectable d ≈ .50 (primary sample 236 vs 36).
  • 2026-09-04 · Exploration E1–E8 run as listed, all eight approved by you. Equivalence tests (E5) added as the formal way to report null results; E7b's mean-rank comparisons voided because the option sets differ.

Statistical concepts

Statistical concepts

Mean and standard deviation SD

Plainly: the mean is the average level; the SD is how spread out people are. An SD of 1.0 on a 7-point scale means most people fall within 1 point of the mean; an SD of 1.8 (A's AU1) means large disagreement. Why now: when comparing two groups the difference has to be read against the spread — a 0.3-point difference is medium when the SD is 1.0 and almost invisible when it is 1.8. Common mistake: reading means without the SD and n.

95% confidence interval CI

Plainly: the sample mean is one estimate of the “true mean”; the CI gives a range showing how precise that estimate is. More people and a smaller SD give a narrower interval. Formal definition: if the same study were repeated many times and an interval computed each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true value. How to read it: A's OH interval [4.99, 5.68] is twice as wide as H's [5.44, 5.78] because A has only 44 people. Common mistakes: overlapping intervals do not mean “no significant difference” (a slight overlap can still be significant); and one cannot say “there is a 95% probability the true value is in this interval”.

Cronbach's α (internal consistency)

Plainly: if several items measure the same thing, their answers should rise and fall together; α measures that agreement (0–1). Why now: to decide whether OH1–3 may be averaged into one OH score. Rules of thumb: ≥ .70 acceptable, ≥ .80 good; but a very high α may only mean the items repeat each other (PE's .96 has that flavour), and α does not prove the items measure a single dimension. Common mistake: treating a low α as a broken scale — with few items α is naturally lower.

Floor and ceiling effects

Plainly: when many people give the top score (7), there is no room to go higher. Consequence: real differences are compressed, the distribution skews left, and means and SDs describe it poorly. What to do: report the share choosing 7, and use ordinal models for robustness (1–7 as ordered categories rather than equally spaced numbers).

Unit of analysis, repeated measures and nesting

Plainly: one person answered three clips, and the three answers resemble each other because they come from the same person. Treating them as three independent people triples the sample size. The mixed model gives each person their own baseline (a random intercept) and estimates condition effects on top of it. That is what the (1 | participant) term means.

Randomisation and covariate balance

Plainly: random assignment makes groups the same “on average”, but any one sample can be imbalanced by chance (age and GAAIS here). Handling: no deletions, no regrouping; add the pre-measures as covariates in a secondary model and see whether conclusions change. Note: only variables measured before the manipulation may be used this way; BEL1, measured after, may not.

p-values and “significance”

Plainly: the p-value answers “if the true difference were zero, how likely is a difference at least this large by luck alone”. p = .004 means such luck occurs about four times in a thousand. α = .05 is a convention, not a law of nature: p = .051 and p = .049 provide almost the same evidence. It does not answer: how large the difference is (see d) or “the probability the hypothesis is true”. Common mistake: reading p > .05 as “no effect” — it only means “these data cannot separate it from zero”.

Effect size Cohen's d

Plainly: how many standard deviations apart two group means are. 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large is only a rough yardstick. The C1 effect on AU1, d = .62: a typical A participant is 0.6 SD below a typical human-condition participant, about 0.8 points on the 1–7 scale. The confidence interval of d, [.26, 1.02], shows how imprecise the estimate is — A has only 36 people, so the interval is wide.

ICC and the likelihood-ratio test LRT

ICC: the share of total variance that lies “between people”. An ICC of .66 means knowing who answered explains two thirds of the differences in scores. LRT: compares the log-likelihoods of two nested models (one with an extra set of parameters); twice the difference approximately follows a chi-square distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of extra parameters. It answers “is this set of parameters useful as a whole”, e.g. “does the condition factor have any effect”, “does the interaction have any effect”.

Contrasts and interactions

Contrast: one number formed by adding and subtracting cell means with weights, e.g. C1 = mean of the six human cells − A. Its test asks “is this number zero”. Contrasts are more powerful than pairwise comparisons because they pool related cells. Interaction: whether one factor's effect changes with another, e.g. “does A's penalty differ across the three clips”. Simple effect: the interaction taken apart, the effect within each clip. Only when the interaction test is significant may simple effects be called “different”.

Unequal variances, the bootstrap and odds ratios

Unequal variances: groups differ in spread. A's participants disagree more; a standard model treats everyone as equally spread and understates the uncertainty of A's mean. Bootstrap: resample participants with replacement within each condition thousands of times, recompute the contrast each time, and look at its distribution — no equal-variance or normality assumption. Odds ratio OR: the effect size of logistic regression, the ratio of the odds of an event between two groups; OR .47 means the odds of the human operator being ranked first in HA are 47% of those in H.

Manipulation checks, credibility checks, and HARKing

Credibility check (BEL1): did participants believe the description — it passes when belief is equal across conditions. Manipulation check: did the description change the perception it was meant to change — here carried by CR3 (HA sees the operator as less in control). Directional hypothesis: predicts the direction of a difference and decides between one- and two-tailed tests; we use two-tailed throughout. Preregistration: publicly registering hypotheses and analyses before seeing the data; without it, the substitute is what this workbook does — writing down the primary sample, outcomes, model and contrasts before any p-value is seen, and labelling everything later as exploratory. HARKing: presenting hypotheses formed after seeing the results as if they had existed beforehand; the only difference from exploratory analysis is honest labelling.

Moderation and simple slopes

Plainly: “does the effect differ between people”. A product term “human × attitude” is added to the model; its coefficient is the difference between the two groups' slopes, and significance means the slopes differ. Simple slopes / conditional effects: the group difference at a given attitude value (e.g. 1 SD below and above the mean). Common mistake: concluding from a significant interaction that “AI-positive people prefer AI” — that needs the difference at +1 SD itself to be significant, and here it is not.

Post-treatment variables are not ordinary moderators

BEL1 is measured after the manipulation and may be a result of the condition: someone in A who found the interaction genuine may for that very reason disbelieve that “the AI is in control”. Grouping on it uses part of the outcome as a grouping variable. So it can only serve sensitivity analyses (does the conclusion hold among believers), not causal claims like “the effect is concentrated among believers”.

Equivalence tests TOST

Ordinary tests ask “is the difference zero” and cannot “prove sameness”. TOST first fixes a bound for “small enough not to matter” (here ±0.35 or ±0.50 SD), then runs two one-sided tests: is the difference significantly above the lower bound and significantly below the upper one. If both are significant, equivalence can be claimed — equivalently, the 90% confidence interval lies entirely inside the bounds. The bounds must be set before looking at the data; we used the smallest detectable effect from the sensitivity analysis.

Ranking data: why mean ranks mislead, and what Plackett–Luce computes

H has 3 options and HA 4: the same actor's mean rank is naturally larger in HA, so comparing mean ranks across conditions is invalid. Plackett–Luce treats a ranking as “pick the first from all actors, then the second from the rest…” and estimates each actor's “worth”, summing to 1 within a condition, so 3-option and 4-option conditions can be compared on the same scale.

Bookkeeping of exploratory tests

The exploration phase ran 113 tests. At a 5% false-positive rate, about 6 would show p < .05 even with no effects at all. So an exploratory finding is judged not only by its p but by whether the direction is consistent across related outcomes (E1 yes), whether one cell drives it (E8 yes, dropped), and whether it survives a change of method (E6's position interaction did not, dropped). All tests are kept in CSV and belong in the paper's supplement.

How large an effect this sample can see (sensitivity)

Plainly: sample size decides how small a difference can be found reliably. In Cohen's d (difference divided by SD; 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large), with 80% power and α = .05: “human vs AI-only” (primary sample 236 vs 36) detects d ≥ 0.50, H vs HA (118 vs 118) detects d ≥ 0.36, disability disclosed vs no mention (159 vs 77) detects d ≥ 0.39, two profile levels (about 78 vs 80) detect d ≥ 0.44, and one condition vs one condition (43 vs 43) needs d ≥ 0.60. So among the 21 pairwise comparisons many real small differences will be “non-significant” — non-significant is not no effect, the keynote of the interpretation.

Open decisions

Open decisions

1Storyline. Two options: (a) the trial storyline “bringing the human back”; (b) an equivalence story opening with disability (see the last paragraph of Appendix A). Both use the same analyses; they differ in the order of the Results and the emphasis of the Discussion. Option (b) needs Study 2's data to answer “do the clips carry a no-disability signal”.

2Study 2 data. If collection has started, send the export; the clip-neutrality check (how many infer a disability, how many infer an AI, with no description) comes first, then the storyline decision.

3More participants. Not recommended for the existing cells. If the disability effect must be tested, open a separate preregistered replication cell with a stronger disclosure (repeated, visible) and a pre-stated sample size and analysis.
